# Vānarajātaka (Ja 342)

**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Vānarajātaka* (Ja 342; also titled *Vānarajātakam*) is a birth story of four verses (*catūhi gāthāhi*) grouped within the *Atthavagga* of the Pali Jātaka collection [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883]. The framing narrative (*paccuppannavatthu*) is set at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana) in Rājagaha, where the Buddha relates the story concerning Devadatta’s schemes to murder him [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), set in Bārāṇasī during the reign of King Brahmadatta, the Bodhisatta lives as a monkey in the Himavanta region [Appleton 2010; Fausböll 1883]. A crocodile befriends him, but the crocodile's pregnant wife develops a craving to eat the monkey's heart [Anandajoti 2010; Appleton 2010]. The crocodile persuades the monkey to ride on his back across the water, but when he reveals his deadly design and tries to drown him, the Bodhisatta outwits him by claiming that monkeys hang their hearts in the branches of trees rather than carrying them inside their bodies [Anandajoti 2010; Appleton 2010]. Believing this ruse, the crocodile returns him to the bank, whereupon the monkey escapes, delivers four verses on practical wisdom, and disappears into the woods [Anandajoti 2010; Appleton 2010; Fausböll 1883]. At the conclusion, the Buddha identifies the crocodile as Devadatta and the clever monkey as himself [Fausböll 1883].
The Bodhisatta's deception in this tale is recognized by modern scholars as posing a distinct ethical problem regarding truthfulness (*sacca*) [Appleton 2010]. In the canonical *Cariyāpiṭaka* (*Kapirājacariya*, III.7), the story was deliberately rewritten under the heading of *sacca-pāramī* to assert that the Bodhisatta spoke no untruth [Morris 1882; Appleton 2010]. The narrative was also transmitted into later vernacular literature, notably appearing as the *Hædaya Vastuva* in the fourteenth-century Sinhalese *Pansiya Panas Jātaka Pota* [Appleton 2010].
SuttaCentral notes structural and thematic parallels to other trickster fables in the collection, specifically Ja 383 (*Kukkuṭajātaka*), Ja 419 (*Sulasājātaka*), and Ja 448 (*Kukkuṭajātaka*) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus registers extensive Pali-internal text reuse between this text and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Tatiyo bhāgo) across four passages, as well as automatic cross-language alignments with Haribhaṭṭa's *Jātakamālā* (*Haribhaṭṭajātakamālā*, D4152) in the Tibetan Tanjur [DharmaNexus].
**Parallels and text reuse**

- Resembling parallels (SuttaCentral): Ja 448 Kukkuṭajātaka; Ja 383 Kukkuṭajātaka; Ja 419 Sulasājātaka
- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Tatiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a3) (§0.4–4.4 ↔ §1057_11–1069)
- Cross-language matches (DharmaNexus): སེང་གེ་ཞབས་འབྲིང་པའི་སྐྱེས་པ་རབས་ཀྱི་ཕྲེང་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ། (haribhaṭṭajātakamālā-nāma) (D4152) [bo]
